data.title: Tlmače – Festunok, a Slavic hillfort at the Slovenská brána
data.excerpt: The Festunok hillfort — older names „Festung“ and „Hradze“ — occupies a rocky peninsula 24 m above the right bank of the Hron at the southern entrance to the Slovenská brána, in the cadastral area of Kozárovce. Its timber-and-earth rampart with an outer stone wall, 560 m long and enclosing 1.84 ha, and a double gateway so far unknown from any other site make it a key part of the 9th–10th-century system of hillforts guarding the route up the Hron.
data.metaTitle: Tlmače – Festunok, a hillfort at the Slovenská brána
data.metaDescription: The Festunok hillfort guards the southern entrance to the Slovenská brána between the Žitava and the Hron, with a 560 m rampart and a double gateway.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A rocky peninsula above the right bank of the Hron (24 m above the water), at the entrance to the Slovenská brána between Tlmače and Kozárovce

keyFacts.label: Dimensions
keyFacts.value: An irregular quadrangle of 150 × 190 m, rampart 560 m long along its crest, area of the hillfort 1.84 ha

keyFacts.label: Construction of the rampart
keyFacts.value: A timber-and-earth rampart (320–330 cm wide) with a wall of quarried stone (140–150 cm) on the outer side, total width 470–500 cm; 5–6 m high from the bottom of the ditch

keyFacts.label: Double gateway
keyFacts.value: A distinctive solution of the entrance — two gateways (10 m and 6 m wide) separated by a paved forecourt, so far unknown from other sites

keyFacts.label: Sacrificial stone
keyFacts.value: In the middle of the hillfort a stone 2 m long, 1 m wide and 1 m high, surrounded by a small rampart

keyFacts.label: Neighbouring hillforts
keyFacts.value: Grác (Pipíška, Malé Kozmálovce), Krivín (Rybník, five enclosures) and the Beňadická skala — together they formed the defensive system of the Slovenská brána

keyFacts.label: State of preservation
keyFacts.value: As late as the mid-20th century one of the six best-preserved hillforts in Slovakia, later parcelled out into vineyards and garden allotments

timeline.title: The earliest occupation
timeline.description: The earlier part of the hillfort, without fortification (or with a fortification later destroyed by the builders), made use of a terrace protected on two sides by a natural slope and on the third by an almost vertical rock face.

timeline.year: end of the 8th – beginning of the 9th century
timeline.title: Warriors' graves at Malé Kozmálovce
timeline.description: Graves with a sword of Carolingian type, stirrups and spears attest to the presence of warriors in the surroundings of Kozárovce even before the hillforts were built.

timeline.title: The Slavic fortification is built
timeline.description: The later part of the hillfort with its rampart (total length 560 m, area 1.84 ha) and a double entrance gateway; the pottery finds show that the last inhabitants were Slavs.

timeline.title: Part of the system of hillforts of the Slovenská brána
timeline.description: Together with the hillforts Grác, Krivín and the Beňadická skala it formed a system guarding the important route from the south into central Slovakia towards the ore deposits — according to J. Dekan the eastern frontier of the Principality of Nitra.

timeline.title: The abbey at Hronský Beňadik is founded
timeline.description: Prince Gejza I founded the abbey so as to have control of the strategic entrance to the north of Slovakia, to the mining towns, through the Slovenská brána.

timeline.title: Fighting between the imperial army and the Turks
timeline.description: The imperial army of General Louis de Souches had its station on the meadows of Kozárovce and on Festunok, from where on 19 July it launched an attack in the direction of Čajkov and Levice.

timeline.title: Janšák's description of the hillfort
timeline.description: Štefan Janšák documents the hillfort and its archaeological finds in his work Staré osídlenie Slovenska (The Ancient Settlement of Slovakia).

timeline.title: Archaeological excavation by A. Habovštiak
timeline.description: The excavation produced a reconstruction of the rampart of the 9th–10th-century hillfort at Tlmače.

timeline.title: The hillfort is parcelled out
timeline.description: The hillfort, which as late as the mid-20th century was among the six best preserved in Slovakia and had survived 1,000 years in good condition, was parcelled out into vineyards and garden allotments.

children.text: The Festunok hillfort (known in older records as „Festung“ or „Hradze“) is a spur of the hill country rising between the rivers Žitava and Hron. It lies between Tlmače and Kozárovce, on the right bank of the Hron, in the cadastral area of the village of Kozárovce. These hills were once part of the Štiavnica mountains, from which they were separated by the Hron. By its erosive action the river created here an interesting geographical formation known as the Slovenská brána (the Slovak Gate). Its remains were so prominent and conspicuous that they were recorded even by cartographers of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

The Festunok hillfort is situated at the southern entrance to the Slovenská brána, one side of which is formed by the Tlmače rock with the hillfort mentioned above, and the other by the hill Kusá hora. The hill with the hillfort (24 m above the level of the Hron) has the character of a rocky peninsula, projecting into the floodplain of the Hron and falling steeply away on three sides. The hillfort consisted of two parts: a later one, well fortified with ramparts and ditches, and an earlier one without fortification. The earlier Neolithic hillfort without fortification (or perhaps with fortifications that were destroyed by the later builders) had all the advantages offered by a high-rising terrace protected on two sides by a natural steep slope (towards the Hron) and on the third side by an almost vertical rock face.

children.text: The hillfort consisted of a circuit rampart in the shape of an irregular quadrangle with main axes measuring 150 × 190 m; it was formed by a massive rampart which on the southern side ran in a gentle curve above the steep slope of the rocky hill. In the north-eastern part the fortification was interrupted by the entrance to the hillfort, which was secured partly by a rampart thrown out in front of the fortification and partly by a projecting length standing outside the circuit rampart, shifted into the interior of the hillfort and joining the main circuit rampart at its northern end. In this way a kind of forecourt with two entrance gateways arose in the area of the entrance, of which the first was 10 m wide and the second 6 m. A distinctive feature of the hillfort at Kozárovce is the individual solution of its entrance by means of a double gateway, created partly by the interruption of the circuit rampart on the eastern side, partly by a projecting length of rampart running eastwards and by a small outwork rampart built parallel with the eastern rampart just above the break of slope. The inner area between the two gateways, which forms a kind of forecourt of the hillfort and through which the road into it led, was paved with small stones. A solution of the entrance to a hillfort by means of a double gateway with a simple rampart fortification is so far not known from other sites.

children.text: The northern and western parts of the fortification were formed by a continuous massive rampart with a pronounced ditch on the outer side; the ditch continued for a short stretch on the southern side as well. Secondarily, the fortification was interrupted only in the south-western part, in order to make access to the area of the former hillfort easier from the southern side too. On the outer side the rampart was 5–6 m high (measured from the bottom of the ditch) and on the inner side 2–3 m. The ditch was dug only on the northern, the western and part of the southern side, that is, where the fortification was not also protected by a slope or a rock face (its average depth was 1.5–2 m). The total length of the rampart along its crest was 560 m and the area of the hillfort 1.84 ha. The fortification on part of the eastern side (at the entrance) and on the northern and western sides consisted of a timber-and-earth rampart and of a stone wall on the outer side. The timber-and-earth part, 320–330 cm wide, consisted of dumped earth and layers of wooden beams laid in the manner of a grillage construction both across and along the rampart. Large quarried stones were laid at the base of the rampart. The timber-and-earth construction was in all probability finished on the inner side with a wall of horizontal beams held by vertical posts. The stone wall on the outer side, built of quarried stones — andesite tuff and occasionally also sandstone — laid dry, was 140–150 cm wide, so that the total width of both parts of the rampart came to 470–500 cm. In the middle of the hillfort there was a sacrificial stone about 2 m long, 1 m wide and 1 m high, which lay on an east–west axis. Around the sacrificial stone there was a small rampart.

children.text: The pottery finds suggest that the last inhabitants were Slavs. The manner of building the fortification described above was common among the western Slavs — with minor variations conditioned partly by the configuration of the terrain, partly by the sources of building material. In the territory of present-day Slovakia, ramparts with a timber grillage construction and a stone wall on the outer side have been recorded at several sites with Slavic hillforts. Hillforts with a similar character of fortification are also known from Moravia, Bohemia and Poland.

According to J. Dekan, and in agreement with Cosmas's accounts, these hillforts are supposed to have formed the eastern frontier of the Principality of Nitra. For understanding and explaining the function of the hillfort at Kozárovce, however, its geographical position and its overall situation within the wider surroundings are of the greatest importance. The hillfort lies in a strategically very significant and important place, directly at the entrance to the Slovenská brána, through which an important route led from the south into central Slovakia, into the region of rich ore deposits. Such an important passage had to be watched and protected, or rather a fortification had to be built beside it which in times of enemy attack would serve as a strategic point and also as a refuge for the population of the immediate surroundings. It was not, however, the only one in this area. At no great distance (about 1 km) to the south of it are the remains of the hillfort Grác on the hill Pipíška in the cadastral area of Malé Kozmálovce, very similar in position and extent and so far not investigated in any detail.

blocks.alt: A reconstruction of the rampart based on the archaeological excavation by A. Habovštiak, 1968

children.text: Another fortified settlement in the Slovenská brána, or rather on its eastern side, may have been the hillfort Krivín opposite Psiare in the cadastral area of the village of Rybník: its rampart fortification differs from that of the other hillforts in the Hron region mentioned so far (it is divided into five enclosures), and finds of a character similar to those from the hillfort at Kozárovce come from it. Almost opposite the previous one lies a fortified settlement unknown until recently — the hillfort on the Beňadická skala. It has the same rampart construction as the one at Kozárovce, and similar finds of the 9th–10th century were recorded on it. If, then, in the area of the Slovenská brána, in a territory whose length does not exceed 7 km, we find at least four hillforts which, by their elevated position and immediate proximity to the route running up the Hron region, and also by the overall character of their occupation and their building technique, display a striking kinship, nothing remains but to regard them as a single whole and system. Like the other related hillforts in the area of the Slovenská brána, the hillfort at Kozárovce had a strategic and guarding as well as an offensive function. The archaeological confirmation of the correctness of such an understanding of the function of the hillfort at Kozárovce and of the whole area of the Slovenská brána may also lie in the finds of iron arrowheads, which are certainly connected with the warrior and guarding activity of its inhabitants. Evidence of the presence of warriors in the wider surroundings of Kozárovce already before the hillforts mentioned above were built may be the find of warriors' graves with a sword of Carolingian type, stirrups and spears, of the end of the 8th or the beginning of the 9th century, at Malé Kozmálovce.

Prince Gejza I, later king of Hungary, was also aware of the strategic position of the Slovenská brána, and in 1075 he founded an abbey at Hronský Beňadik so as to have control of the entrance to the north of Slovakia, to the mining towns. Even long after its demise the hillfort was used for military purposes. On 17 July 1664 fighting began on the Hron between the imperial army and the Turks. The imperial army under the command of General Louis de Souches had its station on the meadows of Kozárovce and on Festunok, from where on 19 July it launched an attack in the direction of Čajkov and Levice.

As late as the middle of the twentieth century the Festunok hillfort was among the six best-preserved hillforts in Slovakia. The hillfort had survived 1,000 years in very good condition. But the comrades decided otherwise and parcelled the hillfort out into plots for vineyards and garden allotments.
